out.other_title: Complexity model of debate: polynomial-time judge, computationally unbounded debaters
out.rationale: The authors credit their analogy to complexity theory to Irving et al., who, for debate, replace the human judge with a polynomial-time algorithm H that outputs one bit. The authors re-apply the analogy to reward modeling: with polynomially bounded quantifiers and a formula that can be evaluated in polynomial time, the agent is like a nondeterministic execution proposing a solution that the user evaluates in deterministic polynomial time, as for NP-complete problems, and from first-order statements with a finite number of alternating quantifiers they suggest that recursive reward modeling can cover a very general space of tasks. That is building on the cited framework with a stated change, so EXTENDS; no theorem is proved here.
out.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Whether a polynomial-time evaluator can supervise harder problems through recursion or interaction; holds only as an analogy, with the user's evaluation treated as a binary polynomial-time predicate

text: When using polynomially bounded quantifiers and a formula that can be evaluated in polynomial time, the authors say reward modeling is analogous to solving NP-complete problems: a nondeterministic execution (analogous to the agent) proposes a solution that can be evaluated for correctness in deterministic polynomial time (by the user). They credit this analogy to complexity theory to Irving et al. (2018) and draw two insights from it: the wide belief that P and NP are not equal supports Assumption 2 that for a lot of relevant problems evaluation is easier than producing solutions, and since basically every formal statement that mathematicians care about can be written as a first-order logic statement with a finite number of alternating quantifiers, this suggests that recursive reward modeling can cover a very general space of tasks.
title: Leike et al. apply Irving et al.'s complexity-theory analogy to recursive reward modeling
